title: Stack vs Heap
concept: The stack is automatic but small; the heap is manual but vast

steps.title: Including stdio.h header
steps.explanation:
We include `#include <stdio.h>` to use `printf`.

This lesson compares the different roles of the stack and the heap.

steps.title: Including stdlib.h header
steps.explanation:
We include `#include <stdlib.h>` to use `malloc`/`free`.

Heap memory is managed directly through functions from this header.

steps.title: Defining the main function
steps.explanation:
The main frame is created.

Now we will compare a stack array and a heap allocation in the same code.

steps.title: Declaring an array on the stack
steps.explanation:
An integer array is created on the stack.

Stack memory is fast and automatically freed, but has a limited size.

steps.title: Allocating memory on the heap (malloc)
steps.explanation:
`malloc` requests a large contiguous block of memory on the heap, and stores the starting address in a pointer.

The actual data lives on the heap; only the pointer holding the address remains on the stack.

steps.title: Checking heap allocation success
steps.explanation:
We check whether the allocation succeeded with `heapArr != NULL`.

Dereferencing a NULL pointer is dangerous, so checking before use is essential.

steps.title: Printing success message
steps.explanation: We print the heap allocation success status.

steps.title: Freeing heap memory (free)
steps.explanation:
`free(heapArr)` returns the heap memory back to the system.

Dynamic allocations must always be paired with a corresponding free.

steps.title: Program termination
steps.explanation:
The program ends with `return 0;`.

Key point: The stack is automatic; the heap requires manual management.

quiz.question: In which situation should you use the Heap?
options: When storing just a single variable (int)
For temporary variables that can disappear when the function ends
When you need to create a large array whose size is determined dynamically at runtime
When you need the fastest possible speed
quiz.explanation: When the array size is not known at compile time (dynamic), or when dealing with very large data, you should use the heap.

misconceptions.wrong: The heap is faster than the stack
misconceptions.why: The stack is a simple structure managed directly by the CPU, while the heap requires complex algorithms to search for free space.

keyTakeaway: Small and fast? Use the stack. Large and long-lived? Use the heap.
